messages.subject: Adjusted sampling: data set up ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

greetings.
Would somebody know at what page number of the DS book (which one) I could
find a hint on how to set up a table, and how to exactly enter data, for
adjusted sampling in DS ?

So, we do a straight line transect til we 'hit' the animals, and then do
intensive DS zig zag'ing til we loose them again; continuing with a straight
line transect afterwards til the next patch is found.

Surveys are done by plane, and line length is easy to compute for us in a
GIS.

Should I stratify the data by 'straight line' vs. 'zig zag' or break the
overall transect line into smaller units/intervals (which then would take
care of the spatial survey intensity via line effort, right) ?

Thanks so much for any advice; very best

   F.

Falk Huettmann PhD, Assistant Professor
-EWHALE lab- Biology and Wildlife Dept., Institute of Arctic Biology
419 IRVING I, University of Alaska Fairbanks AK 99775-7000 USA
Email ff...@uaf.edu  Phone 907 474 7882 Fax 907 474 6716

messages.subject: Re: Adjusted sampling: data set up ?
messages.body_plain:
Falk, adaptive distance sampling methods aren't available in Distance at
this point.  The methods, together with the necessary formulae, are in
chapter 8 of the advanced distance sampling book, and in

Pollard, J.H., Palka, D. and Buckland, S.T. 2002.  Adaptive line
transect sampling.  /Biometrics/ *58*, 862-870.

Unless your population has a very patchy distribution, the expected gain
in precision is likely to be small, so that you may not want to deal
with the extra complexity of the methods.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: move line 0 ?
messages.body_plain:
I have been doing aerial surveys of hunters and have had to address this
same issue.  We plot locations using a tablet pc linked to a GPS so the
observers plot the hunter locations directly on a map. What we have done is
left-truncated the data. In practice I have found that you can identify the
truncation points based on a histogram of distances hunters are observed
(from the transect line).

Our methods are described in:

Stedman, R. S., D. R. Diefenbach, C. B. Swope, J. C. Finley, A. E. Luloff,
and H. C. Zinn.  2004. Integrating wildlife and human dimensions research
methods to study hunters.  Journal of Wildlife Management 68: 762-773.

Diefenbach, D. R., J. C. Finley, A. E. Luloff, R. Stedman, C. B. Swope, H.
C. Zinn, and G. J. San Julian.  2005.  Bear and Deer Hunter Density and
Distribution on Public Land in Pennsylvania.  Human Dimensions of Wildlife
10:201-212.

We make sure the observers are aware of the issue you identified and have
them try to be as consistent as possible when searching for hunters (in how
they sit, hold their head, etc.). I have found when looking out the side
window of a single engine plane, the angle at which you can see closest to
the transect line is pretty consistent.

The bottom line, is whatever approach you use you have to assume that at
whatever distance your observations start the detection probability is 1.0.

Quang and Lanctot (Biometrics - I think they are cited in either the Intro
or Advanced DS books) assumed the detection was 1.0 at some distance from
the plane and modeled a non-monotonic function. That's another approach, but
they were flying at very low elevation and likely did not see everything
close to them (because of the speed issue and blurring of near images).  Our
aerial surveys are done at 600-1,000 feet AGL and that is not a problem.

Duane

Duane R. Diefenbach, Ph.D.
Unit Leader and Adjunct Associate Professor of Wildlife Ecology
U.S. Geological Survey
Pennsylvania Cooperative Fish & Wildlife Research Unit
Pennsylvania State University
404 Forest Resources Bldg
University Park, PA 16802
814-865-4511 (phone)
814-863-4710 (fax)
ddief...@psu.edu
http://pacfwru.cas.psu.edu

-----Original Message-----
From: Wildlife abundance estimation using distance sampling techniques.
[mailto:DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK] On Behalf Of Falk Huettmann
Sent: Tuesday, 16 October, 2007 04:56 PM
To: DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK
Subject: [DIST-SAMP] move line 0 ?

Hi,

one more question, if allowed:

for plane surveys, would it be 'valid' to move the line (0) by a few
angles/meters ?
And if so, by how many degrees/meters (offset) ?

I have not seen this done before, and instead would simply deal with it as
left truncation.

However, as long as the 0 line is clearly (and consistently) defined, this
should not matter much neither; right ?

My concern would come in though with looking from above at the area, line,
with a skewed angle.

Such situations come up for instance when using planes that have no
transparent bottom.

Any suggestions would be welcome; thanks so much and very best

      F.

data with aerial surveys.

messages.subject: Pooled vs. stratified for repeated transects
messages.subject_clean: Pooled vs. stratified for repeated transects
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

We conducted a pilot study on white-tailed deer line transect surveys on
several Wildlife Management Areas and I have a question about the best
way to analyze the data.  The surveys were conducted at night using
spotlights from roads.  I realize that we are violating the assumptions
of the line transect method by using roads as transects, although many
of the "roads" are narrow, sandy trails through the woods and many have
very limited public access and therefore limited use.  However, we do
recognize the problem of using roads and therefore will be careful as to

how to interpret our density estimates. =20

The question I have is how to analyze the data when a transect is
surveyed multiple times (e.g. 5 transects surveyed 6 times per
transect).  I have read the section on pooling the data in Introduction
to Distance Sampling (IDS) on pp. 79 and 294 as one way to deal with
this.  The other alternative is given in the User Guide Distance 5.0
Release 2 in Chapter 8, page 104.  It recommends post-stratifying on the

time (=3Da survey night) period column in the observation data layer or =

in
the sample data layer.  It mentions the problem with variance estimation
when using this method (each stratum is treated as independent when they

are not). =20

As an example, we ran one set of data (3 transects, 10 replicates, total

observations (clusters) =3D193) using both the pooling and the

post-stratification method (in both observer and sample data layer).
When we post-stratified, we tried both setting the strata as replicates
and not as replicates and we estimated the global density as "mean of
stratum estimates weighed by total effort in stratum."  The global
density estimates we obtained using the pooled or the post-stratified
methods were the same.  However, the %CV of the global density estimate
decreases by about 20% when time replicates are treated as replicate
(random) strata instead of pooling the data; the %CV decreases by about
23% from the pooled-data value when time strata are treated as fixed
effects. Correspondingly, the confidence band widths are about 45%
narrower than the pooled-data values when the time strata are treated as
random replicates and about 48% narrower than the pooled-data values
when strata are treated as fixed effects.  Of course, these differences

correspond to differences in the declared degrees of freedom. =20

The treatment on pp. 79 and 294 in IDS of same-transect time replicates
by pooling the data hints at no theoretical qualms about doing so, and
this has been reinforced by at least one fairly recent thread that I've
read on the distance listserv archive.  On the other hand, unless I've
overlooked it, the Distance 5.0 User's Guide does not mention pooling
data from repeat same-transect surveys, but only describes (in Chapter
8, p. 104) treating same-transect repetitions in time as replicates
(either as fixed or random effects), with the caveat that each stratum
in each time period is treated as independent when it is not.   Does
this treatment in the User's Guide reflect a change in the recommended
approach to same-transect survey replicates (despite the caveat about
variance) since the IDS book was written?  Any clarification as to what

would be the preferred method would be greatly appreciated. =20

Again, I realize that we are dealing with a far-from-ideal survey
design; with limited numbers of transects and by using roads.  This year
our attempt was simply to try out the method along with the annual
spotlight surveys using our existing spotlight routes and protocols
(e.g. number of replications).  The next step would be to obtain as
random coverage as possible of each area using a larger number of short
transects (which we have done in some "experimental" areas).  However,
this type of change can take quite some time to be implemented

statewide.    =20

If you would prefer to respond to my email directly, I will post the

summary of the discussion to the list.              =20

Thank You,=20
Elina Garrison
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission=20

Fish and Wildlife Research Institute

4005 South Main Street, Gainesville, FL  32601         =20
Email: Elina.G...@MyFWC.com=20

Phone: (352) 955-2230 ext. 112 / SunCom 625-2230

Fax: (352) 955-2183                                 =20
Visit our website at:  MyFWC.com=20

messages.subject: Re: Pooled vs. stratified for repeated transects
messages.subject_clean: Pooled vs. stratified for repeated transects
messages.body_plain:
Elina, the procedure in IDS is the appropriate one.  Post-stratifying by
occasion is OK if you need separate estimates of abundance for each
occasion, but these separate estimates are not independent, so if you
combine them to get an overall estimate of mean density assuming they
are independent, you will underestimate variance - as you found.  (If
you had a different set of randomised transects for each visit, then
stratification by visit would be OK.)

Steve Buckland
